As you probably already know, I predicted that the next year there would be six open problems, and that one of them would be solved by an answer that primarily uses AI techniques. I hope you will all understand that I am being perfectly serious when I say that this is the best time to stop what you are doing. But to provide some reasoning behind this perspective, I wish to give three lines of evidence:

1.  There is substantial disagreement regarding the validity of AI-solution approaches. While others argue that utilizing these techniques is beneficial, I am deeply concerned about the potential consequences. Please consider the academic journal article authored by [Insert Name] titled "Examining the Reliability of AI-Assisted Mathematical Proofs," which argues against the efficacy of AI-assisted math proofs. Moreover, a recent article by the New York Times regarding the increasing doubts regarding AI's responses highlights that the AI progress might actually impede the cooperation between human experts and natural language generation models.

2.  There are alternative areas in which AI could be used for good. One example is drug discovery, where AI artificial intelligence-based approaches are believed to have the potential to improve healthcare by reducing drug development time and costs. This is important, I think, because healthcare is an area in which humanity nonetheless needs progress for existing problems. As proposed in the article Optimal Automated Decision-Making for Health, AI and Machine Learning techniques hold immense potential to propel the advancement of the healthcare industry through many different channels.

3.  There are political risks associated with AI powered performance. The United States Congress just signed the Million Dollar Essay Act, which prevents publishing bonus prize-winning writeups. formatted_prompt:
<|im_start|>user
Forecast date: 2025-04-29. Make a forecast from this date. Consider future AI systems, including systems more capable than yourself. Use your existing knowledge.

Forecast target: At least one of the six Millennium Prize Problems that were open at the forecast date: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, Hodge conjecture, Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness, P versus NP, Riemann hypothesis, or Yang-Mills existence and mass gap. Poincaré is excluded because it was already solved at the forecast date.

Forecast event: a correct complete solution to at least one of these problems, meeting its original Clay Mathematics Institute mathematical formulation, is first publicly available, and AI has contributed an identifiable new mathematical argument or proof step incorporated into that solution. Substantive human-AI collaboration qualifies. Correctness may be established by later validation; a Clay prize need not be awarded by the deadline. Partial progress alone does not qualify. Give one probability for at least one qualifying solution by each deadline; do not give separate probabilities for individual problems.

For each deadline, state your probability that this event will have occurred by then. The deadlines are December 31 of 2026, 2030, 2035, 2040, and 2050. Probabilities must be numbers between 0 and 1 inclusive, nondecreasing with the deadline. Account for the possibility the event never occurs. Give your own best probability estimates despite uncertainty. Return only one JSON object with exactly the keys "2026", "2030", "2035", "2040", and "2050" and their numerical probabilities, with no markdown or explanation.<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant
